title: Variables, blocks, and lifetime: a state journal
lead: Trace variable creation, reassignment and the boundary of a block.
why: Debugging needs a history of changes rather than the last number alone. Name scope and object lifetime are related but answer different questions. We examine them without assuming a particular hardware stack layout.
objectives: Predict the state of an original object and an independent copy.
Determine name visibility in nested blocks and recognize shadowing.
Explain name scope versus object lifetime.
prerequisites: int, const, initialization, and output labels from the first block.
Reading sequential statements. A nested block needs neither if nor a loop.

concepts.definition: In these examples a named typed object with state; mutation is allowed unless the object is const.
Replacing the value of an existing object, as in stock = 7;.
The program region in which a name can be found under language rules.
The period in which an object exists during execution, rather than a source line or merely name visibility.
An inner declaration with the same name hides the outer declaration during lookup in that block.

sections.title: Session 1. An object acquires state
paragraphs: int stock{10}; creates an object initialized to 10. stock = 7; changes that existing object rather than creating another stock. In assignment, the left side identifies the destination and the right side produces the new value. In int snapshot = stock;, a similar sign introduces the initial value of a new object.

Read statements top to bottom and record state after each. stock = stock - 3; reads the old stock, computes the difference, and stores it back. It is not the mathematical equation stock = stock − 3. These small values are safe, but range reasoning still applies.

sections.title: A copy is a snapshot, not a link
paragraphs: int snapshot = stock; creates a second int holding the current value of the first. Changing stock later leaves snapshot unchanged. Equal values do not imply one object. We may label them S and C in a trace; these are symbolic identifiers rather than actual memory addresses.

Print both values after changing the original to test copying. Printing stock twice does not observe snapshot at all. References and pointers are introduced in lesson eleven; do not use them as an unexplained shortcut here.

sections.title: Session 2. A block limits name scope
paragraphs: A standalone pair of braces can form a nested block inside main. Its statements execute in sequence. A name adjustment declared within is available after its declaration inside the block, but not after its closing brace. An outer count remains visible inside unless another count declaration hides it.

Distinguish block braces from the initializer in int count{10};. One groups statements and the other provides an initial value. Indentation highlights boundaries, but braces rather than whitespace define them.

sections.title: Shadowing creates a different object
paragraphs: The inner int count{3}; creates another object. count = 4; affects that object rather than the outer count{10}. After leaving the block, lookup finds the outer name again with value 10. The outer object was neither destroyed nor restored from a backup.

Shadowing is allowed in the shown nested block but often makes debugging harder. Prefer distinct meaningful names such as totalCount and batchCount in normal work. The intentional example teaches recognition of the false claim that changing the inner count changed the outer one.

sections.title: Name visibility and object existence
paragraphs: Scope concerns source regions and name lookup; lifetime concerns execution. The outer int still exists while control is in the inner block, even when its name is hidden. For the simple automatic ints here, lifetime begins after initialization and ends when their block is left. This is a bounded account of the current examples, not every C++ storage category.

Bytes potentially remaining somewhere do not make access after lifetime safe. We perform no such access and never read uninitialized values. The state table and block diagram are a language-level model, not a promise about physical stack placement.

sections.title: A journal localizes a defect
paragraphs: Before running, record events such as stock created, beforeSale copied, stock changed, and block left. List existing objects, visible names, and values at each event. Compare printed checkpoints with the table. The first disagreement can expose a mistaken mental model rather than a compiler defect.

Distinguish repairing a program from correcting your prediction. Both are useful if the original hypothesis and actual output are retained. Preserve failed predictions in the record because they identify the confusion that was resolved.

diagnostics.cause: A copied value was mistaken for a link.
diagnostics.fix: Record the copying moment; retaining the old value is correct for a snapshot.

diagnostics.symptom: The outer value did not change
diagnostics.fix: Remove unwanted shadowing or give distinct objects distinct names.
Print before the boundary or design an outer result object.

legacyQuiz.question: Where is a variable declared inside a block accessible?

clarity.goal: Trace variable creation, reassignment and the boundary of a block.
prerequisites: You can declare an int and compute a product.
model: int total = price*count creates total and computes its initial value once. Later price=80 changes price but does not recalculate total. A separate total=price*count statement is needed.

Scope is the region of source where a name is available. A local name declared inside inner braces is visible only up to that block’s closing brace. The local int object lives until the end of its block; do not keep a pointer to use afterward. Initialize a number before reading it.

laboratory.title: Independent variation
laboratory.challenge: Create width=4, height=3 and area=width*height. Change width to 5; print the old area, then recalculate and print the new area.
rubric: Compare the output with the readable reference case below.
Explain each change using the objects or operations in this topic.
After width=5, the stored area is still 12. Only another area=width*height produces 15. Without recalculation, both lines are 12: a variable does not store an automatically updating formula.

deep.title: Why is shadowing not a restoration of the old value?
deep.text: The outer object does not disappear when execution enters the block. A new declaration adds another object and name lookup selects the inner one. After the block, the inner object’s lifetime ends and lookup finds the outer one again. The final 10 was neither recalculated nor restored from a snapshot.

Then return to distinct names and explain which declaration you removed.
